title: What Federalism Is
hook: Some countries split authority between a national government and regional ones, each with powers the other can't simply override.
key_points: Federalism divides power between a central government and regional units (states, provinces, or länder).
Each level has its own areas of authority, often set out in a constitution.
It contrasts with a unitary system, where the central government holds ultimate power.
Examples include the United States, Germany, India, and Canada.
content_html: Federalism is a way of organizing a country so that authority is shared between a central, national government and a set of regional governments — called states, provinces, länder, or similar names depending on the country. The defining feature is that each level has its own sphere of authority, usually spelled out in a written constitution, so the national government cannot simply abolish the regional ones, and vice versa.
extra_html: This contrasts with a unitary system, where ultimate power rests with the central government and any regional bodies exist at its discretion. Federalism is often adopted in large or diverse countries, where it lets different regions manage local matters while a national government handles shared concerns like defense or currency. Encyclopaedia Britannica describes how federal arrangements work and how they vary; well-known examples include the United States, Germany, India, and Canada. The next card looks more closely at how federal and unitary systems compare.

related.title: Unitary vs Federal Systems
related.hook: Where does the final say live — with one national government, or shared with regions? That choice shapes how a country is run.

related.title: Separation of Powers
related.hook: Split government into branches that make, enforce, and interpret the law — so no single part can do all three.

related.title: Local Government
related.hook: The layer of government you meet most often isn't the national one — it's the city or council that runs your streets, schools, and rubbish collection.

related.title: Devolution & Confederation
related.hook: Between a single central government and a loose alliance of states lies a spectrum — and where power sits on it shapes who can really decide.

related.title: When Federal Law Overrides the States
related.hook: Who decides what warning goes on a bottle of weed killer — a state jury or the federal government? The answer turns on a quiet but powerful rule called preemption.

flashcards.prompt: What does federalism divide power between?
flashcards.back_html: A central (national) government and regional units such as states or provinces, each with its own areas of authority.

flashcards.prompt: How does a federal system differ from a unitary one?

choices.text: In a federal system regional units have protected powers; in a unitary system the center holds ultimate power
Federal systems never hold elections; unitary ones do
There is no real difference between them

flashcards.explanation_html: Federalism guarantees regional units their own authority; in a unitary system that authority ultimately rests with the central government.

flashcards.prompt: Which is commonly cited as a federal country?

choices.text: A country with only one national government and no regional powers

flashcards.explanation_html: Germany, like the US, India, and Canada, is federal — power is shared with regional units (its länder).
